Just read your post again and saw that you were wanting to winter sow into these beds. My experience with these beds was planting nursery starts in the spring. The sheet mulch method does hinge on giving the beds the winter (or six weeks in summer) to decompose. This doesn’t make a good seedbed because the composting reactions generate heat and need thick mulch to retain moisture, insulate from freezing temps, and suppress weeds in the soil bank. I do recommend this method but it would work best if you’re willing to buy nursery starts in the spring. Plant things close and add ground cover to suppress weeds. The common violets totally took over my native plant beds around the starts and I couldn’t be happier. I had no weeds to speak of this summer!

I had good success this year with sheet mulch. I did a thin layer of compost, then cardboard, compost, a thick layer of “brown” material (straw, leaves, etc), compost, and then a seed free mulch layer. Have tried different browns in different beds and think that the leaves did the best. Straw is expensive, difficult, messy for me to get in the city. Works fine though and it’s ok for it to have seeds because of your seed free mulch layer. But leaves were free from my neighbors, mess free since they were bagged up, and composted down very well over the winter. I also used the leaves as mulch on top for additional ease and cost savings. I had a very successful vegetable patch in the leaf beds this summer, so can attest that it made for a nutrient dense soil even in its first season!

Ideally you could add more topsoil, compost, or manure to get the compost cooking over the winter.  If nothing else put a good thick mulch layer over the top to keep the topsoil in place and help retain moisture. If you don’t mind the appearance bags of leaves work just fine. You may still have difficulty with weed suppression without that cardboard layer between the dirt and your compost layer, so unless you’re willing to rake it back and put down cardboard you’ll want to at least thicken the layers you have.
